title: The Watchful Father of the House

text: Simon Åke Strandvik and Anna Sophie Schedin now own the property at Valinge Rygg 24 in Varberg. The sellers are Anneli Maria Josarp, Jan Eric Sawarell, Greta Gunilla Lundqvist, Leif Anders Nilsson, Kjell Yngve Nilsson, Monica Birgitta Elisabeth Nilsson, Mari Helena Nilsson, Lise-Lotte Gabriella Nilsson, Karl Jörgen Nilsson, Ihrene Elisabeth Marguerite Aspling, Ann-Louise Ljungquist, Anna Maria Nilsson, and Lars-Göran Nilsson.

The charming residential house was built in 1909 and is located in a scenic, secluded setting at the end of the road in Valinge. The property has a rich history and has over the decades served as home to several generations of local families, but has over time also accommodated newer businesses. Today, the property – with the historical designation Rygg 3:7, now Rygg 24 – includes the main house and three barns. It is a vibrant location offering accommodation as well as space for courses, events, and celebrations.

The estate is not only a place for relaxation and smaller gatherings, but also serves as the stage for the intimate, private music festival FestiValinge. The festival was hosted in August 2026, featuring live bands, DJs, and an open stage in the garden and barn.

In recent times, visitors and friends who have stayed overnight or house-sat at the property have recounted strange and unusual occurrences. Several people have both heard and seen phenomena indicating a continued presence on the estate. Among other things, people have noticed a man who seems to walk around, tidying up and keeping things in order in the house – closing doors that were left open, with the clattering of dishes heard from the kitchen as if someone is standing there washing up. These experiences have mainly occurred when the owners were away and others were house-sitting, as if the man is also there to look after the property and keep a watchful eye over Lunden.

Sometime during the 1960s, the property was taken over by a Danish man (and his wife/partner). In connection with the change of ownership, a comprehensive full renovation was carried out, and during their time on the estate, they ran a dog boarding kennel, among other things. Following this period, the house later stood empty, which unfortunately led to its decay – before the current owners took over, put in significant effort, and brought Lunden back to life.

Arthur William Sixten Nilsson was born on March 23, 1910, in Abild and moved into the house on November 8, 1943. He worked as a milk recording inspector (kontrollassistent), and the household also included his wife Junis Linnéa (née Gustavsson), born on June 4, 1914, in Varberg. They married on November 20, 1937, and had daughters Siv Elsa Anita (born February 25, 1938), Gerd Harriet Irène (born December 19, 1940), and Gudrun Elsie Margaretha (born November 29, 1945). The family also included their son Gösta, who was born in the 1950s and is therefore not listed in the older parish registers. Arthur passed away on June 13, 1986, and Junis on February 1, 1998; the couple rests together at S:t Jörgen's Cemetery.

During Arthur's time, the property was expanded significantly. On April 3, 1945, the Nilssons purchased a parcel of land of nearly 0.75 hectares (the so-called marsh parcel, 'kärrskiftet') from the neighboring property Rygg 6:1 for 1,400 SEK. The area was partitioned off and officially merged with Lunden (Rygg 3:7) in June 1946, growing the property to just over 1 hectare – a land purchase made so they could keep a cow on the farm.

Before Arthur and his family took over, the house was owned and inhabited by the carpenter Johan Andersson, born on June 1, 1898, in Valinge. He was married to Anna Hildegard (née Johansson), born on July 15, 1902, in Valinge. The couple married on February 10, 1922, and it was in connection with their wedding that they took over the property. They had two daughters: Astrid Junia (born March 4, 1922, died March 12, 1997) and Inga-Marianne (born December 6, 1935). On October 20, 1944, the whole family moved out to settle in Lindberg. Johan passed away in 1968 and Anna on February 28, 1993. Johan is buried in Valinge alongside his wife and their eldest daughter Astrid.

Before Johan took over, the house was owned by his father, Sven Edvard Andersson, born on February 9, 1858, in Valinge and passed away on December 30, 1938. It was Sven who had the house built on November 25, 1909. He lived there with his wife Hilma Maria Johansdotter, born on May 26, 1856, in Lindberg and passed away on July 4, 1926. They married on November 23, 1881, and had their son Johan. The household also included Augusta Josefina Andersdotter (born March 6, 1856, died June 10, 1918), who was likely a sister of Sven. Sven continued to live with Johan and his family until his death. Sven is buried in Valinge alongside his wife and two other female relatives, possibly sisters.

The Lunden property has its historical roots in May 1905, when landowner Nils Aron Carlsson sold a land area of 28 ares and 3 square meters (approx. 0.28 hectares) from the main property 1/4 mantal Kronoskatte Rygg No. 3 (Bengt Olsgård) for 1,000 SEK to carpenter Johan Helander Karlsson. The Land Survey Office in Halmstad confirmed the land division on August 12, 1905, under the property designation Rygg 3:7.

It was thereafter, around the year 1909, that the current residential house was erected on the site by Sven Edvard Andersson, who later acquired the property before his son Johan Andersson took over upon his marriage in 1922.

Going even further back in time, we find Sven's father, Carl Petter Larsson (born August 6, 1830, in Valinge), who was a tenant farmer (torpare) at Rygg 4. Sven's mother was Johanna Andersdotter, born on December 28, 1818, in Valinge. Besides Sven, the children included sister Matilda (born October 23, 1863) and brother Johan Anton (born June 22, 1856), who later moved to Rolfstorp in 1875. When Sven's mother Johanna passed away on April 16, 1883, father Carl Petter remarried Britta Christina Bengtsdotter (born September 24, 1833) from Lindberg.

history.heading2: Historical Events and Legends in Valinge Parish
text: People have lived in the Valinge area for at least 3,000 to 4,000 years. The district is rich in remnants from the Bronze Age and the Migration Period. The name was previously spelled Hvalinge. The word 'hval' is Old Norse for ridge or wall, meaning the name refers to those living by the ridge.

One of the major milestones in the parish's modern history was when the old medieval stone church in Valinge was demolished in 1886. In 1891–1892, the current church was completed in a proud Neo-Romanesque style. The construction was a major event for the entire community, requiring extensive efforts and transport from all the tenant farmers and landowners in the parish. However, the church tower was retained from an earlier rebuilding in 1840 and still bears King Karl XIV Johan's initials (C XIV J) in ironwork on its facade.

During the 19th century, the Great Enclosure reform (laga skiftet) was carried out in Valinge parish, fundamentally altering the cultural landscape. Previously, houses were clustered tightly in village cores, but with the enclosure, villages were split up, and families moved their homes and outbuildings directly out to their assigned land parcels. It was this historical reform that laid the foundation for individual small homesteads – like Lunden at Rygg – to emerge and be partitioned.

Everyday life in the countryside was also marked by hardships and disease. On March 20, 1814, four children died in epidemics of whooping cough and measles in the Varberg area – childhood diseases that claimed many young lives in Halland during this time. In Valinge, Lundby was among the places affected when ten-month-old infant Johannes Börjesson died of whooping cough.

The parish's older history also contains dramatic individual court cases. In the local court records archive, an incident from the Great Northern War in 1711 is documented, where a baggage train driver (trossdräng) in Valinge suffered a tragic death that was brought before the district court. It is one of the oldest recorded crime and tragedy notes documented in local historical research.

During World War II, Valinge unexpectedly found itself at the center of events. On October 10, 1943, a large Allied Liberator Mk.III bomber aircraft (belonging to the Royal Air Force) crashed in a field in the parish. The plane was returning from a special mission when it ran out of fuel. The entire crew of seven Polish aviators managed to bail out by parachute north of Rolfstorp before the abandoned plane crashed.

In 1959, the community was shaken by the so-called 'Valinge Strike', when church caretaker Gustaf Nilsson went on strike. This led to a prolonged and bitter labor dispute that attracted widespread attention. The strike became famous for its dramatic events where strike-breakers ('blacklegs') were reported to dig graves under the cover of darkness so burials could take place despite the blockade.

In Halland folklore, there are also traces of old legends about terrifying creatures, including the Gloson – a feared sow ghost with glowing eyes and a saw-toothed back. According to belief, the sow appeared on dark winter nights and posed a particularly dangerous threat to anyone venturing out for the traditional 'year walk' (årsgång).

One of the more classic folk legends from the area is recorded in the folklore archives. It is told that while a picture of the Devil was being painted in Valinge church, the Devil himself appeared before the painters and hissed: 'No matter how hideous you paint me, I can make myself even more hideous!'
